lesson_title: Two Pages and a Spine: Triangle Rules in 2D and 3D
hook_text: How tall is the tower nobody can climb? Two friends, one measuring tape and two triangles answer it from the ground.
clip_script: A tower you cannot climb. Two friends stand 100 metres apart on the ground, and that is all the equipment this needs. Here is the secret of every 3D question: there is no such thing as a 3D triangle. There are two FLAT triangles pretending — one lying on the ground, one standing upright, joined along a shared side like two pages of an open book. Solve the lying page first, because that is where the data lives: ground angles 70 and 50, so 60 at the tower, and the sine rule hands over the spine — the flat distance from friend to tower base, 88 comma 4 6 metres. Now carry that number up the standing page. Friend B looks up at the top: 25 degrees. Right angle at the base, tangent finishes it: 88 comma 4 6 times tan 25 — the tower is 41 comma 2 5 metres tall. Nobody left the ground. Data page first, spine across, answer page second. That order cracks every tower, every flagpole, every 3D question on the paper.
visual_style: A cellphone tower on open veld, two friends with a measuring tape, the scene folding flat into two paper triangles hinged along a glowing shared edge, numbers travelling across the hinge.
mood: Heist-movie clever, grounded, one clean reveal of the height.
pacing: A slow look up the impossible tower, brisk confident steps through the ground triangle, a rising finish as the height snaps into place.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and take the fear out of every 3D triangle question.
